messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Questions about warmup
parts:
Some questions about warmup:

1. Are the warmup iterations for a) adapting computational parameters (mass matrix, etc.), b) for convergence/burnin, or c) for both?

2. Assuming that a) or c) is the answer, how do you know whether or not you allowed enough warmup iterations to get the computational parameters sufficiently adapted? When I've done MCMC that used a Metropolis-Hastings update for some variable, I could get an idea of whether I adapted the proposal distribution width long enough by taking a look at the acceptance rate and seeing if the proposal distribution width has stabilized. I don't know what the equivalent would be for NUTS.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Questions about warmup
parts:
On 11/5/13, 10:15 PM, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> Some questions about warmup:
>
> 1. Are the warmup iterations for a) adapting computational parameters (mass matrix, etc.), b) for convergence/burnin, or
> c) for both?

In the default random inits case, both.

You can always initialize at a converged point to avoid (b).

And you can turn adaptation off and avoid (a).

> 2. Assuming that a) or c) is the answer, how do you know whether or not you allowed enough warmup iterations to get the
> computational parameters sufficiently adapted? When I've done MCMC that used a Metropolis-Hastings update for some
> variable, I could get an idea of whether I adapted the proposal distribution width long enough by taking a look at the
> acceptance rate and seeing if the proposal distribution width has stabilized. I don't know what the equivalent would be
> for NUTS.

NUTS is a form of Metropolis-Hastings if that helps. And it suffers
from the same diagnosis difficulty as standard random-walk Metropolis
Hastings, namely that you can get good acceptance one of two ways, either
by adapting the proposal distribution well or by lowering the step size.

What you want to see is good effective sample sizes. And we recommend
evaluating multiple chains to give you some confidence that you've
converged to the right location. Michael also recommends making a final
run with a much higher target acceptance rate (which is what's tuned
during adaptation) to force a lower step size to diagnose problems with
the posterior that might not be evident through R-hat stats or effective
sample size estimates.

They also share the same problem when using global adaptation that they
don't adapt to local curvature, as in the funnel example of Neal's.

There are more details in the original NUTS paper, more details
in the manual, and many more details to come in a string of papers
being written by Michael Betancourt and various collaborators.

Michael's also breaking down the warmup iterations more finely to
allow a bit of convergence before trying to adapt the mass matrix
(which plays the same roll as the covariance matrix in random-walk
Metropolis).

-Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Questions about warmup
parts:
1. Are the warmup iterations for a) adapting computational parameters (mass matrix, etc.), b) for convergence/burnin, or
c) for both?

In practice HMC converges to the typical set really, really fast so the majority of our warmup period is actually spent

(a) Filling the chain with samples from the typical set (this is only important if you think about a Markov chain as the set of states, and not just the current state)

(b) Learning the (co)variances in order to update the metric.

Because (b) can have such a huge impact on performance, especially for NUTS, we put a nontrival amount of time into warmup
even if technical convergence was really fast.

2. Assuming that a) or c) is the answer, how do you know whether or not you allowed enough warmup iterations to get the
computational parameters sufficiently adapted? When I've done MCMC that used a Metropolis-Hastings update for some
variable, I could get an idea of whether I adapted the proposal distribution width long enough by taking a look at the
acceptance rate and seeing if the proposal distribution width has stabilized. I don't know what the equivalent would be
for NUTS.

NUTS is a form of Metropolis-Hastings if that helps.  And it suffers
from the same diagnosis difficulty as standard random-walk Metropolis
Hastings, namely that you can get good acceptance one of two ways, either
by adapting the proposal distribution well or by lowering the step size.

What you want to see is good effective sample sizes.  And we recommend
evaluating multiple chains to give you some confidence that you've
converged to the right location.  Michael also recommends making a final
run with a much higher target acceptance rate (which is what's tuned
during adaptation) to force a lower step size to diagnose problems with
the posterior that might not be evident through R-hat stats or effective
sample size estimates.

They also share the same problem when using global adaptation that they
don't adapt to local curvature, as in the funnel example of Neal's.

There are more details in the original NUTS paper, more details
in the manual, and many more details to come in a string of papers
being written by Michael Betancourt and various collaborators.

Michael's also breaking down the warmup iterations more finely to
allow a bit of convergence before trying to adapt the mass matrix
(which plays the same roll as the covariance matrix in random-walk
Metropolis).

As written NUTS is technically a slice sampler, but that's a very pedantic point.

You can look at the distribution of the accept_stat (the average acceptance probability
over the NUTS subtree) but you'll find that's it's not particularly unimodal.  In most
cases it's actually bimodal, which is perfectly acceptable but just makes visual diagnostics
more difficult.

Because HMC updates the parameters jointly looking at any marginal statistic
is only going to give you limited information.  As Bob recommended your best
indication that "everything is working well" is N_eff / N_total no less than 10%.
There's lot of information deep within NUTS that can say more, but it requires
lots of experience with the algorithm and the theory and difficult to generalize
to a generic diagnostic.
